claim: Moment-to-moment neural variability has been shown to scale positively with the complexity of stimulus input.
source: Moment-to-moment neural variability has been shown to scale positively with the complexity of stimulus input.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research establishing this relationship

claim: Participants expressed higher variability when viewing more complex visual stimuli.
source: We replicated previous findings that participants expressed higher variability when viewing more complex visual stimuli.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the current study replicating prior findings

claim: Variability modulation was associated with higher baseline visual GABA levels.
source: Additionally, we found that such variability modulation was associated with higher baseline visual GABA levels and was reduced in older adults.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing correlation between GABA levels and variability modulation

claim: Variability modulation was reduced in older adults.
source: Additionally, we found that such variability modulation was associated with higher baseline visual GABA levels and was reduced in older adults.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing younger and older adults

claim: Participants with lower baseline GABA levels showed a drug-related increase in variability modulation when pharmacologically increasing GABA activity.
source: When pharmacologically increasing GABA activity, we found that participants with lower baseline GABA levels showed a drug-related increase in variability modulation while participants with higher baseline GABA showed no change or even a reduction, consistent with an inverted-U account.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from pharmacological intervention study

claim: Participants with higher baseline GABA showed no change or even a reduction in variability modulation when pharmacologically increasing GABA activity.
source: When pharmacologically increasing GABA activity, we found that participants with lower baseline GABA levels showed a drug-related increase in variability modulation while participants with higher baseline GABA showed no change or even a reduction, consistent with an inverted-U account.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from pharmacological intervention study

claim: The drug-related effects on variability modulation are consistent with an inverted-U account.
source: When pharmacologically increasing GABA activity, we found that participants with lower baseline GABA levels showed a drug-related increase in variability modulation while participants with higher baseline GABA showed no change or even a reduction, consistent with an inverted-U account.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental data in light of theoretical framework

claim: Higher baseline GABA and variability modulation were jointly associated with better visual-discrimination performance.
source: Finally, higher baseline GABA and variability modulation were jointly associated with better visual-discrimination performance.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing correlation between GABA, variability modulation, and behavioral performance

claim: GABA plays an important role in how humans utilize neural variability to adapt to the complexity of the visual world.
source: These results suggest that GABA plays an important role in how humans utilize neural variability to adapt to the complexity of the visual world.
evidence: Inference drawn from the combined experimental findings

claim: An efficient neural network may modulate neural dynamics to align with the complexity of input stimuli.
source: It has been postulated that an efficient neural network may do this by modulating neural dynamics to align with the complexity of input stimuli; neural dynamics would be increased to process more complex stimuli, but compressed to process less complex stimuli (Hermundstad et al., 2014; Orbán et al., 2016; Garrett et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical and empirical work

claim: SDBOLD is a far more powerful predictor of cognitive abilities than the traditionally used mean-BOLD signal changes.
source: In fact, research so far has demonstrated that SDBOLD is a far more powerful predictor of cognitive abilities than the traditionally used mean-BOLD signal changes (Garrett et al., 2013b; Garrett et al., 2011; Grady and Garrett, 2014) (including in the domain of stimulus selectivity Garrett et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Regional BOLD variability can drive the strength of functional connectivity measures.
source: Our recent work (Krohn et al., 2023) shows that regional BOLD variability can even drive the strength of functional connectivity measures (another popular fMRI measure).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent work

claim: The ability to upregulate visuo-cortical SDBOLD when viewing more complex, feature-rich visual stimuli characterized those with better visuo-cognitive performance in older adults.
source: Although age comparisons have not yet been made, recent research only in older adults found that the ability to upregulate visuo-cortical SDBOLD when viewing more complex, feature-rich visual stimuli characterized those with better visuo-cognitive performance (Garrett et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research in older adults

claim: The modulation of variability in response to task demands is reduced in older adults compared to younger adults.
source: Moreover, previous research suggests that the modulation of variability in response to task demands is reduced in older adults compared to younger adults (Garrett et al., 2011; Garrett et al., 2010; Garrett et al., 2013a) and that this reduction is associated with poorer behavioral performance (Garrett et al., 2010; Garrett et al., 2013a; Grady and Garrett, 2018; Waschke et al., 2021; Rieck et al., 2017; Rieck et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Reduction in variability modulation is associated with poorer behavioral performance.
source: Moreover, previous research suggests that the modulation of variability in response to task demands is reduced in older adults compared to younger adults (Garrett et al., 2011; Garrett et al., 2010; Garrett et al., 2013a) and that this reduction is associated with poorer behavioral performance (Garrett et al., 2010; Garrett et al., 2013a; Grady and Garrett, 2018; Waschke et al., 2021; Rieck et al., 2017; Rieck et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: GABA has been associated with cortical plasticity.
source: GABA has been associated with cortical plasticity (Jones, 1993; Hensch et al., 1998; Fagiolini et al., 2004) with pattern complexity (Monteforte and Wolf, 2010) and with the dynamic range Shew et al., 2011; Agrawal et al., 2018 of neural networks.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: GABA has been associated with pattern complexity.
source: GABA has been associated with cortical plasticity (Jones, 1993; Hensch et al., 1998; Fagiolini et al., 2004) with pattern complexity (Monteforte and Wolf, 2010) and with the dynamic range Shew et al., 2011; Agrawal et al., 2018 of neural networks.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: GABA has been associated with the dynamic range of neural networks.
source: GABA has been associated with cortical plasticity (Jones, 1993; Hensch et al., 1998; Fagiolini et al., 2004) with pattern complexity (Monteforte and Wolf, 2010) and with the dynamic range Shew et al., 2011; Agrawal et al., 2018 of neural networks.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Altering the strength of inhibitory connections in artificial neural networks can dramatically affect moment-to-moment dynamics and the number of different states that networks can sample.
source: Computational work has found that altering the strength of inhibitory connections in artificial neural networks can dramatically affect moment-to-moment dynamics and the number of different states that networks can sample (Agrawal et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to computational modeling work

claim: Decreasing GABA activity pharmacologically in healthy young rats and monkeys leads to a decrease in network dynamics and reduces the number of states visited by the cortical network.
source: Similarly, decreasing GABA activity pharmacologically in healthy young rats and monkeys leads to a decrease in network dynamics and reduces the number of states visited by the cortical network (Shew et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to animal research

claim: GABA levels are lower in older adults.
source: In humans, GABA levels are lower in older adults (Chamberlain et al., 2021; Lalwani et al., 2019; Simmonite et al., 2019; Cassady et al., 2019; Porges et al., 2017a; Chalavi et al., 2018; Hermans et al., 2018; Gao et al., 2013; Cuypers et al., 2018; Levin et al., 2019; Porges et al., 2021; Porges et al., 2017b) and in recent work, we found that overall cortical resting-state SDBOLD can be increased in older, poorer performing adults by GABA agonism (Lalwani et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research in humans

claim: Overall cortical resting-state SDBOLD can be increased in older, poorer performing adults by GABA agonism.
source: In humans, GABA levels are lower in older adults (Chamberlain et al., 2021; Lalwani et al., 2019; Simmonite et al., 2019; Cassady et al., 2019; Porges et al., 2017a; Chalavi et al., 2018; Hermans et al., 2018; Gao et al., 2013; Cuypers et al., 2018; Levin et al., 2019; Porges et al., 2021; Porges et al., 2017b) and in recent work, we found that overall cortical resting-state SDBOLD can be increased in older, poorer performing adults by GABA agonism (Lalwani et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent work

claim: Houses were more 'feature-rich' than faces in both C1 and C2 layers of the HMAX model.
source: To anticipate the results, we found that houses were more 'feature-rich' than faces in both C1 (corresponding to V1) and C2 layers (corresponding to extrastriate regions), as described in detail below, consistent with (Garrett et al., 2020; all t-values>10).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results with statistical significance

claim: House stimuli consistently produced a larger median C1 activation value than faces across all receptive field sizes.
source: The results of these 8 (scales) × 4 (orientations) independent sample t-tests (Figure 1a and c) indicate that houses consistently produced a larger median C1 activation value than faces across all receptive field sizes.
evidence: Supported by statistical tests and shown in Figure 1

claim: House stimuli showed greater median activity compared with faces across different patch sizes in C2 layer.
source: We found that house stimuli showed greater median activity compared with faces across different patch sizes (Figure 1b and d).
evidence: Supported by statistical tests and shown in Figure 1

claim: A single significant latent variable revealed higher SDBOLD when viewing houses than faces, particularly in ventral visual cortex.
source: Using Partial Least Squares (PLS), we found a single significant latent variable (p<0.001) revealing higher SDBOLD when viewing houses than faces (SDBOLD-HOUSES >SDBOLD-FACES), particularly in ventral visual cortex (See Figure 2 for spatial extent peak and Table 1 for further details).
evidence: Supported by PLS analysis with statistical significance and shown in Figure 2

claim: The task-condition effect on SDBOLD was significant in both younger and older adults.
source: This task-condition effect on SDBOLD was significant in both younger (t(57) = 3.43, p<0.001, Cohen's d=0.45) and older adults (t(76) = 4.15, p<0.001, Cohen's d=0.47).
evidence: Supported by statistical tests in both age groups

claim: Raw GABA+/H2O levels were significantly lower in older adults compared to younger adults.
source: Raw GABA+/H2O levels (measured using MR spectroscopy) were significantly lower in older adults compared to younger adults (t (131.9)=–6.6, p=8e-10, Cohen's d=1.1).
evidence: Supported by MRS measurements with statistical significance

claim: GABA+levels were significantly lower in older adults compared to younger adults after correcting for tissue-composition differences.
source: GABA +levels were also significantly lower in older adults compared to younger adults after correcting for tissue-composition differences (t(131.9)=–3.13, p=0.002, Cohen's d=0.53) after applying Harris et al.'s alpha tissue correction procedure (Porges et al., 2017b).
evidence: Supported by MRS measurements with tissue correction and statistical significance

claim: Differences in tissue composition do not explain the observed lower GABA levels in older adults.
source: These results suggest that the differences in tissue composition do not explain the observed lower GABA levels in older adults.
evidence: Inference from tissue-corrected GABA measurements

claim: An Age x GABA interaction was not significant.
source: An Age x GABA interaction was not significant, F(1,120) = 1.07, p=0.3; (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by statistical test and shown in Figure 3a

claim: Individual differences in GABA levels play a role in how individuals modulate brain signal variability.
source: These results suggest that individual differences in GABA levels play a role in how individuals modulate brain signal variability.
evidence: Inference from the correlation between GABA and variability modulation

claim: Tissue-composition corrected auditory GABA+levels were not associated with modulation of visual variability in the whole sample after controlling for age.
source: Further, we found that tissue-composition corrected auditory GABA +levels (see Lalwani et al., 2019 for details of voxel placement) were not associated with modulation of visual variability in the whole sample after controlling for age (F(1,120) = 0.72, p=0.4) or within older adults alone (r(74) = 0.01, p=0.9).
evidence: Supported by statistical tests showing no association

claim: Tissue-composition corrected motor GABA+levels were not associated with modulation of visual variability in the whole sample after controlling for age.
source: Similarly, tissue-composition corrected motor GABA +levels (see Cassady et al., 2019 for details of voxel placement) were not associated with modulation of visual variability in the whole sample after controlling for age (F(1,120) = 0.52, p=0.47) or within older adults alone (r(74) = 0.02, p=0.9), revealing that our GABA +effects were specific to visual cortex.
evidence: Supported by statistical tests showing no association

claim: The GABA effects were specific to visual cortex.
source: Similarly, tissue-composition corrected motor GABA +levels (see Cassady et al., 2019 for details of voxel placement) were not associated with modulation of visual variability in the whole sample after controlling for age (F(1,120) = 0.52, p=0.47) or within older adults alone (r(74) = 0.02, p=0.9), revealing that our GABA +effects were specific to visual cortex.
evidence: Inference from the lack of association with auditory and motor GABA

claim: Age-Group did not interact with GABA level in the drug-related shift in Δ→SDBOLD.
source: Age-Group did not interact with GABA level (F (1,37)=0.9, p=0.36).
evidence: Supported by statistical test showing no interaction

claim: A significant Age-Group x GABA level interaction on visual discrimination behavior was observed, even after controlling for gray matter volume.
source: We also observed a significant Age-Group x GABA level interaction on visual discrimination behavior, even after controlling for gray matter volume (F(1,65) = 7.13, p=0.01, Cohen's f=0.3).
evidence: Supported by statistical test controlling for gray matter volume

claim: GABA levels were more strongly associated with better visual performance in younger adults than in older adults.
source: On examining the interaction further (See Figure 5a), we found that GABA levels were more strongly associated with better visual performance in younger adults (rho(30) = 0.62, p=0.0002, Spearman's correlation) than in older adults (rho(36) = 0.37, p=0.022).
evidence: Supported by correlation analyses in both age groups and shown in Figure 5a

claim: Higher GABA levels were associated with better visual performance in both younger and older adults.
source: Regardless, higher GABA levels were associated with better visual performance in both younger and older adults.
evidence: Supported by correlation analyses in both age groups

claim: Brain signal variability in the visual cortex was modulated during various task conditions (greater when viewing more complex houses vs. less complex faces).
source: First, brain signal variability in the visual cortex was modulated during various task conditions (greater when viewing more complex houses vs. less complex faces).
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: SDBOLD in response to more 'feature-rich' house stimuli was greater than in response to simpler face stimuli in the visual cortex.
source: Consistent with prior research in older adults by Garrett et al., 2020, we replicated the finding that BOLD signal variability (SDBOLD) is modulated based on the complexity of visual stimuli. SDBOLD in response to more 'feature-rich' house stimuli was greater than in response to simpler face stimuli in the visual cortex.
evidence: Replication of prior findings with current data

claim: Neural activity in the visual system should exhibit greater dynamic range in response to more complex input.
source: Our current findings support the hypothesis that neural activity in the visual system should exhibit greater dynamic range in response to more complex input (van Hateren, 1992; Waschke, 2023).
evidence: Interpretation of findings in light of theoretical hypothesis

claim: Greater variance in stimulus features has been argued to drive salience in the visual system.
source: Indeed, greater variance in stimulus features has been argued to drive salience in the visual system (Hermundstad et al., 2014), which in turn could lead to an increase in resource allocation.
evidence: Supported by citation to theoretical work

claim: The visual system reduces resource allocation (narrowing neural dynamic range) when stimulus input is more reducible or less feature rich.
source: It is hypothesized that the visual system (a) reduces resource allocation (narrowing neural dynamic range) when stimulus input is more reducible or less feature rich (here, faces), while it (b) upregulates dynamic range when stimulus input is more differentiated or feature rich (here, houses).
evidence: Theoretical hypothesis about visual system function

claim: The visual system upregulates dynamic range when stimulus input is more differentiated or feature rich.
source: It is hypothesized that the visual system (a) reduces resource allocation (narrowing neural dynamic range) when stimulus input is more reducible or less feature rich (here, faces), while it (b) upregulates dynamic range when stimulus input is more differentiated or feature rich (here, houses).
evidence: Theoretical hypothesis about visual system function

claim: Upregulation of variability in response to the complexity of sensory input may reflect a well-adapted, dynamic neural network.
source: Such upregulation of variability in response to the complexity of sensory input may reflect a well-adapted, dynamic neural network, akin to a 'well-adapted organism', as discussed by Marzen and DeDeo, 2017.
evidence: Interpretation of findings in light of theoretical framework

claim: Older adults may be less able to adapt to processing demands in their environment.
source: Older adults may indeed be less able to adapt to processing demands in their environment (Garrett et al., 2013b; Waschke et al., 2021).
evidence: Inference from current findings and prior research

claim: GABA levels play a role in individual differences in brain signal variability beyond the effects of age or tissue composition.
source: Though both GABA levels and brain signal variability decline with age this relationship was significant even after controlling for age and tissue composition. This suggests that GABA levels play a role in individual differences in brain signal variability beyond the effects of age or tissue composition.
evidence: Inference from statistical analyses controlling for confounds

claim: Having sufficient inhibitory activity to offset excitatory activity has been found to be essential to allow artificial neural networks to operate near criticality.
source: Having sufficient inhibitory activity to offset excitatory activity has been found to be essential to allow artificial neural networks to operate near so-called criticality (Shew et al., 2011; Poil et al., 2012), allowing them to visit a variety of different network states, exhibiting higher dynamic range (Agrawal et al., 2018) and brain signal variability (Lalwani et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to computational and empirical work

claim: Operating near criticality allows neural networks to visit a variety of different network states, exhibiting higher dynamic range and brain signal variability.
source: Having sufficient inhibitory activity to offset excitatory activity has been found to be essential to allow artificial neural networks to operate near so-called criticality (Shew et al., 2011; Poil et al., 2012), allowing them to visit a variety of different network states, exhibiting higher dynamic range (Agrawal et al., 2018) and brain signal variability (Lalwani et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to computational and empirical work

claim: The finding that GABA is related to brain signal variability is consistent with computational modeling showing inhibition affects network dynamics.
source: Our finding that GABA (the brain's major inhibitory neurotransmitter) is related to brain signal variability is consistent with this finding.
evidence: Interpretation of current findings in light of prior computational work

claim: A flexible neural network which can sample a higher number of network states would be able represent different stimuli using a wider variety of different states - leading to more distinct representations of stimuli from each other.
source: A flexible neural network which can sample a higher number of network states would be able represent different stimuli using a wider variety of different states - leading to more distinct representations of stimuli from each other.
evidence: Theoretical reasoning about network function

claim: Lower visual GABA levels in older adults have been associated with less differentiated responses to different visual stimuli in primates and humans.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, lower visual GABA levels in older adults have been associated with less differentiated responses to different visual stimuli in primates (Leventhal et al., 2003) and humans (Chamberlain et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Lower GABA levels in older adults underlie a reduced ability to align neural variability to stimulus complexity, yielding impoverished stimulus differentiation in the older adult brain.
source: Our results extend these findings and suggest that lower GABA levels in older adults underlie a reduced ability to align neural variability to stimulus complexity, yielding impoverished stimulus differentiation in the older adult brain.
evidence: Inference from current findings and prior research

claim: Manipulating GABA levels in healthy rodents leads to a change in neural variability.
source: Indeed, previous research in rodents noted that manipulating GABA levels in healthy rodents leads to a change in neural variability (Shew et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to animal research

claim: These findings provide the first evidence in humans for an inverted-U account of how GABA may link to variability modulation.
source: These findings thus provide the first evidence in humans for an inverted-U account of how GABA may link to variability modulation.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental findings as novel contribution

claim: Higher than optimal levels of inhibition can lead to dampening of the entire network.
source: One explanation is that higher than optimal levels of inhibition can lead to dampening of the entire network.
evidence: Theoretical explanation for observed effects

claim: Reduced neuronal firing decreases the number of states the network can visit and decreases the dynamic range of the network.
source: This reduced neuronal firing decreases the number of states the network can visit and decreases the dynamic range of the network.
evidence: Theoretical explanation for observed effects

claim: Some anesthetics work by increasing GABA activity (for example propofol a general anesthetic modulates activity at GABAA receptors) and GABA is known for its sedative properties.
source: Indeed, some anesthetics work by increasing GABA activity (for example propofol a general anesthetic modulates activity at GABAA receptors) and GABA is known for its sedative properties.
evidence: Established knowledge about GABA and anesthetics

claim: Propofol leads to a steeper power spectral slope in monkey ECoG recordings.
source: Previous research showed that propofol leads to a steeper power spectral slope (a measure of the 'construction' of signal variance) in monkey ECoG recordings (Gao et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Networks function optimally only when dynamics are stabilized by appropriate levels of inhibition.
source: Networks function optimally only when dynamics are stabilized by appropriate levels of inhibition.
evidence: Theoretical principle about network function

claim: Past work arguing for the presence of neurochemical inverted-U effects in humans has rarely estimated baseline neurochemical levels in specific brain regions prior to pharmacological manipulation.
source: It is important to note that past work arguing for the presence of neurochemical inverted-U effects in humans has rarely estimated baseline neurochemical levels in specific brain regions prior to pharmacological manipulation, instead often relying on simple genotyping as a baseline estimate (e.g. COMT as a proxy for baseline dopamine Bäckman et al., 2006) or invasive PET-based imaging (Cools et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research methods

claim: MR spectroscopy may provide the easiest, regionally-specific baseline estimate of GABA for future tests of the GABAergic inverted-U.
source: MR spectroscopy may provide the easiest, regionally-specific baseline estimate of GABA for future tests of the GABAergic inverted-U.
evidence: Inference about methodological implications

claim: The GABA-behavior relationship is consistent with the hypothesis that older adults who maintain neurochemical levels comparable to those in younger adults experience fewer age-related impairments.
source: The GABA-behavior relationship was present in both age groups and is consistent with the hypothesis that older adults who maintain neurochemical levels comparable to those in younger adults experience fewer age-related impairments (Nyberg et al., 2012; Bruffaerts et al., 2019).
evidence: Interpretation of findings in light of theoretical hypothesis

claim: The role of GABA in visual performance is consistent with previous research which found that GABA levels in the primary visual cortex are associated with better orientation discrimination in neurons in corresponding early visual processing areas.
source: The role of GABA in visual performance is consistent with previous research which found that GABA levels in the primary visual cortex are associated with better orientation discrimination in neurons in corresponding early visual processing areas (Kurcyus et al., 2018) and with improved fluid processing ability (Simmonite et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: GABA levels in the primary visual cortex are associated with improved fluid processing ability.
source: The role of GABA in visual performance is consistent with previous research which found that GABA levels in the primary visual cortex are associated with better orientation discrimination in neurons in corresponding early visual processing areas (Kurcyus et al., 2018) and with improved fluid processing ability (Simmonite et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Sensorimotor GABA levels predict motor function.
source: For example, sensorimotor GABA levels predict motor function (Cassady et al., 2019; Levin et al., 2019), auditory GABA levels predict hearing loss (Gao et al., 2015; Dobri and Ross, 2021), and fronto-parietal GABA levels predict cognitive function across multiple domains assessed by higher MOCA scores (Porges et al., 2017a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Auditory GABA levels predict hearing loss.
source: For example, sensorimotor GABA levels predict motor function (Cassady et al., 2019; Levin et al., 2019), auditory GABA levels predict hearing loss (Gao et al., 2015; Dobri and Ross, 2021), and fronto-parietal GABA levels predict cognitive function across multiple domains assessed by higher MOCA scores (Porges et al., 2017a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Fronto-parietal GABA levels predict cognitive function across multiple domains assessed by higher MOCA scores.
source: For example, sensorimotor GABA levels predict motor function (Cassady et al., 2019; Levin et al., 2019), auditory GABA levels predict hearing loss (Gao et al., 2015; Dobri and Ross, 2021), and fronto-parietal GABA levels predict cognitive function across multiple domains assessed by higher MOCA scores (Porges et al., 2017a).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Dopamine levels also affect the modulation of variability during visual tasks.
source: Previous research has found that not only GABA, but dopamine levels also affect the modulation of variability during visual tasks (Garrett et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) balance plays a critical role in network flexibility.
source: Animal research also suggests that excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) balance plays a critical role in network flexibility (Agrawal et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to animal research

claim: Dysfunction in GABAergic signaling has been linked to Alzheimer's disease.
source: Separately, researchers have also found a link between dysfunction in GABAergic signaling and AD (Calvo-Flores Guzmán et al., 2018) as well as poor cognitive functions (Porges et al., 2017a) as described above.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Dysfunction in GABAergic signaling has been linked to poor cognitive functions.
source: Separately, researchers have also found a link between dysfunction in GABAergic signaling and AD (Calvo-Flores Guzmán et al., 2018) as well as poor cognitive functions (Porges et al., 2017a) as described above.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: The study analyzed data from 58 young (age 18–29 years) and 77 older (age 65 and above) adults.
source: We analyzed the data from 58 young (age 18–29 years) and 77 older (age 65 and above) adults who completed the entire MiND study before the start of the COVID-19 pandemic.
evidence: Description of study sample

claim: All participants were recruited from Ann Arbor and the surrounding area, were right-handed, native English speakers, and had normal or corrected to normal vision.
source: All participants were recruited from Ann Arbor and the surrounding area, were right-handed, native English speakers, and had normal or corrected to normal vision.
evidence: Description of participant characteristics

claim: Participants who scored 23 or lower on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MOCA) were screened out.
source: We screened out participants who scored 23 or lower on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MOCA) (Carson et al., 2018).
evidence: Description of exclusion criteria

claim: The study had 80% power to detect a correlation of r=0.47 in each age-group alone.
source: In our convenience sample of those who completed the study before the pandemic and who completed the behavioral tasks (Subset 3), we had 80% power to detect a correlation of r=0.47 in each age-group alone.
evidence: Power analysis calculation

claim: All subjects participated in three sessions, each on a separate day.
source: After completing an initial telephone screening interview and being determined eligible, all subjects participated in three sessions, each on a separate day.
evidence: Description of study design

claim: Session 1 only involved cognitive and behavioral testing, session 2 included a functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scan, and session 3 only involved a Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy (MRS) scan.
source: Session 1 only involved cognitive and behavioral testing, session 2 included a functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scan, and session 3 only involved a Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy (MRS) scan (See Figure 7 for summary).
evidence: Description of study design shown in Figure 7

claim: The first 25 older adults and 20 younger adults enrolled in the study participated in two fMRI sessions (on and off drug) as well as a separate MRS session.
source: The first 25 older adults and 20 younger adults enrolled in the study participated in two fMRI sessions (on and off drug) as well as a separate MRS session (described in detail below).
evidence: Description of subset 1 participants

claim: Participants received either 0.5 mg or 1 mg of benzodiazepine during the on-drug fMRI session and the dosage was randomly assigned independent of their age-group, weight, or height.
source: They received either 0.5 mg or 1 mg of benzodiazepine during the on-drug fMRI session and the dosage was randomly assigned independent of their age-group, weight, or height.
evidence: Description of drug administration protocol

claim: The drug-based component of the study was discontinued after the first-year review in February 2018.
source: The drug-based component of the study was discontinued after the first-year review in February 2018.
evidence: Description of study timeline

claim: A subset of participants completed four visual tasks in noise that are relevant to the current study.
source: We later (June 2018) added more behavioral tests specifically targeting the visual perception in noise (described below in detail). Thus, a subset of participants (subset 3) who enrolled in the study after June 2018 completed four visual tasks in noise that are relevant to the current study and described here along with the off-drug fMRI session and spectroscopy session on separate days (See Table 3 for more details about participant split across sessions and source data file participant demographic details).
evidence: Description of subset 3 participants and tasks

claim: A subset of participants (38 older and 36 younger adults) completed four visual tasks in noise, administered on a Dell laptop with a 15.6-inch screen using the Psychophysics Toolbox.
source: A subset of participants (38 older and 36 younger adults) completed four visual tasks in noise, administered on a Dell laptop with a 15.6-inch screen using the Psychophysics Toolbox.
evidence: Description of behavioral testing setup

claim: All tasks consisted of trials in which a 500ms fixation cross was followed by a black and white picture in dynamic Gaussian noise for 500ms followed by a response screen.
source: All tasks consisted of trials in which a 500ms fixation cross was followed by a black and white picture in dynamic Gaussian noise for 500ms followed by a response screen.
evidence: Description of task structure

claim: Each task began with 4 practice trials with feedback and was followed by 50 scored trials without feedback.
source: Each task began with 4 practice trials with feedback and was followed by 50 scored trials without feedback.
evidence: Description of task structure

claim: The tasks followed a staircase procedure – when a participant made three correct responses in a row, the level of noise was increased.
source: The tasks followed a staircase procedure – when a participant made three correct responses in a row, the level of noise was increased.
evidence: Description of adaptive task procedure

claim: The dependent measure was the average level of noise presented for the last 40 trials.
source: The dependent measure was the average level of noise presented for the last 40 trials.
evidence: Description of behavioral outcome measure

claim: A higher score represents better performance on the visual tasks.
source: Thus, a higher score represents better performance.
evidence: Description of behavioral outcome measure interpretation

claim: A single visual sensory factor was computed based on four tasks using factor analysis.
source: Using the MATLAB function factoran we computed a single visual sensory factor based on these four tasks.
evidence: Description of data analysis method

claim: The task consisted of six 20 s blocks of images of male faces and six 20 s blocks of images of houses, presented in a pseudorandomized order and interleaved with twelve 10 s blocks of a fixation cross.
source: The task consisted of six 20 s blocks of images of male faces and six 20 s blocks of images of houses, presented in a pseudorandomized order and interleaved with twelve 10 s blocks of a fixation cross.
evidence: Description of fMRI task structure

claim: Each block consisted of the stimulus presented for 500ms with an interstimulus interval (ISI) of 500ms.
source: Each block consisted of the stimulus presented for 500ms with an interstimulus interval (ISI) of 500ms.
evidence: Description of fMRI task timing

claim: The block order was the same for all the participants.
source: The block order was the same for all the participants.
